title: Five things grocers need to know about SNAP fraud
summary: SNAP fraud is real, but restricting online purchases is not an effective way to prevent it. Try chip-enabled cards, real-time monitoring, & shared fraud intelligence
body_markdown:
*The policy landscape for SNAP and EBT is changing faster than ever. In this series, we break down the latest developments and what they mean for retailers.*


## Focusing on solutions that work


SNAP fraud is receiving increased news coverage, but payment error rates—often caused by administrative mistakes—are frequently conflated with intentional fraud.


At the same time, a few states have begun blocking online SNAP transactions, even though online purchases have stronger security and traceability controls. Meanwhile, the largest transaction-level threat remains skimming at physical checkout terminals.


What follows are five facts to help retailers separate the headlines from the actual risks—and focus on solutions that work.


1.


**Payment errors are not fraud.** Error rates are receiving attention because new federal cost-sharing rules could make states financially responsible for them. But these rates primarily measure eligibility, calculation and administrative mistakes—not fraudulent transactions.[USDA explanation](https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/qc)


2.


**The largest transaction-level threat is skimming at physical stores.** Criminals capture card data and PINs at brick-and-mortar POS terminals and use cloned cards to drain benefits. GAO documented more than $320 million in replaced stolen benefits from October 2022 through December 2024.[GAO analysis](https://www.gao.gov/blog/stolen-snap-benefits-cost-beneficiaries-millions)


3.


**Online SNAP is designed with stronger security and traceability controls.** USDA requires secure encrypted PIN entry, additional retailer authorization, end-to-end testing and controls on card changes and balance inquiries.[USDA requirements](https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/retailer/online/requirements)


4.


**Default online restrictions target the wrong channel.** They create legitimate declines and customer confusion without stopping skimming or card cloning—and may push shoppers back toward the physical terminals where theft begins.


5.


**Restricting online SNAP runs counter to the program’s direction.** Online SNAP has grown from a pilot into essential infrastructure and is now available in all 50 states and D.C. Congress is advancing proposals to make it a permanent nationwide feature, reflecting its necessity in a digital economy.[USDA program status](https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/online) |[House legislation](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/7567/text) |[Senate proposal](https://www.agriculture.senate.gov/agricultural-act-of-2026-farm-bill-20) Forage's view: SNAP fraud is real, but restricting online purchasing is neither an effective fraud strategy nor sound public policy. Chip-enabled cards, real-time monitoring, shared fraud intelligence and targeted verification offer a better path.
